text:
# Brick-based storage and caching

Also called: Bricking, Brick Caching, Out-of-core Volume Rendering

## Overview
[Brick-based storage](#6680-sparse-chunk-brick-storage.md) and caching decomposes volumetric datasets larger than available GPU texture memory into smaller, fixed-size sub-volumes called bricks, enabling out-of-core visualization by treating GPU memory as a cache for these bricks [S2, unofficial][S3, unofficial][S5, unofficial]. It solves the hardware limitation where a single 3D texture cannot hold the entire volume, ensuring that expensive data transfers from slower host memory are minimized [S4, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly managing the cache lifecycle (e.g., LRU replacement) and handling boundary interpolation via overlap, whereas [Tile-based Volume Ray Marching](1678-tile-based-volume-ray-marching.md) focuses on tile-level traversal and [Spatial Indexing and Ordering](1797-spatial-indexing-and-ordering.md) focuses on [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) structures for traversal rather than memory residency management.

## Shared principles
The family shares the following mechanisms:

1.  **Multi-Resolution Brick Partitioning:** The volume is represented as a hierarchy consisting of multiple resolution levels. Each brick is a chunk of voxel data belonging to a specific resolution level [S1, unofficial].
2.  **Fixed [Voxel Brick](#5794-voxel-bricks.md) Size:** Each brick has a size in voxels (e.g., $32^3$) that is the same for all resolution levels [S1, unofficial]. This size is independent of the brick's spatial extent.
3.  **Spatial Extent Determination:** The spatial extent of a brick is determined solely by the resolution level it belongs to [S1, unofficial]. Unlike the geometric subdivision of a [residency octree](#4950-residency-octree.md), the downsampling ratio between resolution levels in the [bricked volume hierarchy](#5036-bricked-volume-hierarchy.md) is flexible [S1, unofficial].
4.  **GPU Cache Residency:** To access a brick's data on the GPU, it must be resident in a [brick cache](#3222-brick-cache-implementation.md) [S1, unofficial].
5.  **Boundary Padding:** Bricks are typically stored with 1-voxel padding on all sides to support trilinear interpolation at boundaries without accessing adjacent bricks [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial]. The stored [voxel count](#2908-grid-resolution-calculation.md) per brick is:
    $$ V_{brick} = (B_x+1)(B_y+1)(B_z+1) $$
    where $B_x, B_y, B_z$ are the logical brick dimensions [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Brick Caching with LRU Replacement](879-brick-caching-with-lru-replacement.md)
Manages a fixed-size pool of volume data blocks, mapping brick coordinates to pool indices and evicting least-recently-used blocks when the pool is full. It solves the problem of limited GPU memory capacity and transfer bandwidth by ensuring that expensive data transfers from slower host memory are minimized. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly managing the cache lifecycle using a Last Recently Used (LRU) policy, often requiring CPU-side coordination due to the limitations of standard shader models regarding random memory writes. Unlike [Multi-Level Cache and Prefetching](4631-multi-level-cache-and-prefetching.md) which focuses on prefetching, or [Raymarching with LOD-based Brick Caching](5776-raymarching-with-lod-based-brick-caching.md) which integrates caching with LOD selection, this method focuses on the core eviction logic and memory pool management.

### [Bricking](914-bricking.md)
[Bricking](#914-bricking.md) is a memory management technique that subdivides volumetric datasets larger than the available GPU texture memory into smaller, equally-sized sub-volumes called bricks, allowing them to be loaded on-demand and rendered individually. It solves the hardware limitation where a single 3D texture cannot hold the entire volume, enabling out-of-core visualization by treating the GPU memory as a cache for these bricks. Unlike [Brick-based Volume Raycasting](3341-brick-based-volume-raycasting.md), which focuses on the ray traversal logic, or [Dynamic Rebricking](2823-dynamic-rebricking.md), which decouples physical and logical sizes, standard Bricking uses fixed-size bricks for both storage and rendering, relying on overlap and sorting to maintain visual continuity.

### [Level-of-Detail Volume Rendering via 3D Textures](1706-level-of-detail-volume-rendering-via-3d-textures.md)
Level-of-Detail (LOD) Volume Rendering via 3D Textures is a method for interactive visualization of large-scale volumetric datasets by adaptively selecting resolution levels for individual bricks based on visual importance criteria. It solves the problem of texture memory exhaustion and excessive sampling rates in large volumes by constructing a local multi-resolution hierarchy for each brick, allowing regions of interest to be rendered at high resolution while distant or less opaque regions are rendered at coarser levels. Unlike spherical-shell approaches, this method uses planar slicing parallel to the image plane and guarantees continuous interpolation and correct opacity accumulation at brick boundaries through explicit texture adaptation and polygon [clipping](#1444-clipping.md).

### [Brick-based Volume Raycasting](3341-brick-based-volume-raycasting.md)
[Brick-based volume raycasting](#3341-brick-based-volume-raycasting.md) decomposes volume data into fixed-size, power-of-two bricks to achieve high [CPU](#10688-naive-sdf-generation-cpu.md) cache coherency without the memory overhead of spread memory layouts. Unlike linear raycasting, which suffers from view-dependent performance drops due to cache misses, this method provides nearly constant rendering performance regardless of viewing direction. It builds on [Brick-based storage and caching](4138-brick-based-storage-and-caching.md) by defining the specific [ray-marching](#6739-ray-marching.md) algorithm and addressing scheme required to traverse this one-level subdivision hierarchy efficiently.

### [N³-tree with Brick Pool and Node Pool](3407-n-tree-with-brick-pool-and-node-pool.md)
The [N³-tree with Brick Pool and Node Pool](#3407-n-tree-with-brick-pool-and-node-pool.md) is a [hierarchical data structure](#4133-hierarchical-data-structures.md) for voxel rendering that combines an N³-tree for spatial subdivision with a brick pool for volume data and a node pool for [tree structure](#4139-tree-based-structures-octree-pointer-tree-sparse-voxel-dag.md), allowing efficient Level-of-Detail (LOD) and [visibility culling](#6226-visibility-culling.md). It differs from sibling methods like [Brick Caching with LRU Replacement](879-brick-caching-with-lru-replacement.md) by integrating the tree traversal logic directly into the GPU shader using a compact, cache-coherent node representation, and from [Bricked Volume Hierarchy](5036-bricked-volume-hierarchy.md) by using a single pointer per node to reduce memory overhead and improve cache coherence.

### [Multi-Level Cache and Prefetching](4631-multi-level-cache-and-prefetching.md)
[Multi-Level Cache and Prefetching](#4631-multi-level-cache-and-prefetching.md) is a memory management strategy for web-based volume visualization that bridges the gap between persistent storage and high-speed rendering by utilizing a four-tier cache hierarchy and aggressive prefetching. It solves the problem of high-latency remote data fetching (order of 100 ms) in browser environments by ensuring that frequently accessed data slices and chunks are available in faster memory tiers, thereby hiding I/O latency during user interactions such as orbiting or slider playback. It differs from sibling methods like [Brick Caching with LRU Replacement](879-brick-caching-with-lru-replacement.md) by explicitly separating compressed and decompressed states across distinct memory ceilings and leveraging the browser's Origin Private File System (OPFS) for persistent storage, rather than relying solely on volatile GPU or CPU caches.

### [Bricked Volume Hierarchy](5036-bricked-volume-hierarchy.md)
The Bricked Volume Hierarchy is a data organization scheme where a volume dataset is partitioned into chunks called bricks across multiple resolution levels. It solves the problem of managing multi-resolution volume data by decoupling the logical resolution levels from the geometric subdivision of the space. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as the [N³-tree with Brick Pool and Node Pool](3407-n-tree-with-brick-pool-and-node-pool.md), is that the downsampling ratio between resolution levels is flexible, whereas the geometric subdivision in residency octrees is fixed.

### [Raymarching with LOD-based Brick Caching](5776-raymarching-with-lod-based-brick-caching.md)
[Raymarching with LOD-based Brick Caching](#5776-raymarching-with-lod-based-brick-caching.md) is a visualization method for [Compressed Segmentation Volumes](#4985-compressed-segmentation-volume.md) (CSVs) that renders volumes by decompressing bricks on-demand at the required Level of Detail (LOD) and storing them in a GPU cache. It solves the problem of rendering extremely large segmentation volumes by exploiting temporal coherency and detail separation, allowing coarse LOD data to remain on the GPU while fine LOD data is streamed from CPU memory. It differs from its siblings by using a specific cache structure of contiguous base elements rather than superblocks/columns, and by testing palettes for [empty-space skipping](#1002-empty-space-skipping.md) before requesting cache locations.

### Cyclic Buffer for Smoke Volume
- [S1, unofficial] A cyclic buffer structure used to store layers of smoke volume data, where the first layer (Index 0) is duplicated to the end to enable smooth transitions at the seeding step.
- [S1, unofficial] A buffer where the first layer is duplicated to the end to depict cyclic property, allowing overwriting of the oldest layer.
- [S1, unofficial] Each layer has an age relative to the time it was seeded. The oldest layer is overwritten next. When a layer at index 4 is overwritten, it becomes the youngest, and the seeding indicator moves one step forward.
- [S1, unofficial] To enable smooth transitions at the seeding step, the volumes of cubic cells between two layers are multiplied by a fade-in/out modifier based on the age of the cell.
- [S1, unofficial] Overwrite the oldest layer (indicated by an arrow) with new data, moving the seeding indicator one step forward. The overwritten layer becomes the youngest.
- [S1, unofficial] Multiply volumes of cubic cells between two layers by a fade-in/out modifier depending on cell age to enable smooth transitions at the seeding step.

### Homogeneous Brick Optimization
- [S2, unofficial] Nodes corresponding to homogeneous bricks (all voxels contain the same value up to a user-defined threshold) store the average value in the brick instead of a pointer to the brick's location in the brick cache.
- [S2, unofficial] For multi-channel data, a node can only be marked homogeneous if its corresponding bricks in all channels are homogeneous.

## Background
Bricking was introduced to overcome the limitations of 3D texture memory sizes in early GPU hardware (e.g., NVIDIA GeForce 6 with a $512^3$ resolution limit and 256MB memory limit) [S1, unofficial]. The technique allows visualization of volumes that exceed these limits by treating the GPU memory as a cache for bricks loaded from disk [S2, unofficial][S6, unofficial]. The approach has been widely adopted in various forms, including CPU-side LRU caching [S2, unofficial], GPU-side N³-trees [S1, unofficial], and web-based multi-level caching with prefetching [S1, unofficial]. It is used in real-time volume rendering, medical imaging visualization, and scientific data analysis.
